full_prose_under_review.title: Ordering Schedule I and II Stock: DEA Form 222 and CSOS
full_prose_under_review.topic: Controlled substance procurement / Schedule I and II ordering
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: When an order is required, the 60-day window, defective and lost orders, and how each route is preserved
learning_objectives: State when a DEA Form 222 or a digitally signed electronic order is required for a Schedule I or II distribution, and name the movements 21 CFR 1305.03 excepts.
Read the 60-day window correctly: what it runs from, what it permits, and why it is not sixty business days.
Separate a defective order from a lost one, because the two failures have different cures and leave different records.
State how long each ordering record is kept, where it is kept, and what makes an electronic copy count as separately maintained.
Describe CSOS as the electronic equivalent of the paper form rather than a scan of one, and identify the duties that travel with the electronic route.
Name the report a purchaser owes when order forms are lost or stolen, and the one carve-out the regulation writes into it.

orientation.text: Ordering Schedule I and II stock is not dispensing, and the paperwork that governs it is not a prescription. 21 CFR 1305.03 attaches its requirement to a distribution: each distribution of a Schedule I or II controlled substance requires either a DEA Form 222 or its electronic equivalent under subpart C of part 1305 and part 1311. The document therefore sits between two registrants, a supplier and a purchasing pharmacy, and it records a movement of stock rather than a therapy decision. The regulation then lists the movements it does not reach, and the list is short and specific: distributions to persons exempted from registration, exports that conform with the Act, deliveries to a registered analytical laboratory or its DEA-approved agent, delivery from a central fill pharmacy to a retail pharmacy, deliveries to an authorized registrant by an ultimate user or by a long-term care facility on behalf of a resident or former resident or by a person authorized to dispose of a decedent's property, distributions to reverse distributors and distributors by collectors and law enforcement, and deliveries from ultimate users for a recall. Anything outside that list needs an order.

There are two routes to that order and they are alternatives, not a document and a copy of it. On the paper route the purchaser executes a DEA Form 222, the original travels to the supplier, and the purchaser keeps a copy of every executed form under 21 CFR 1305.17, together with copies of any unaccepted or defective forms and the statements attached to them. That the supplier holds the original is visible in the failure provisions themselves, since both 21 CFR 1305.15 and 21 CFR 1305.16 describe the supplier sending an original back to the purchaser. On the electronic route the purchaser signs an order with a digital signature DEA issued to the purchaser or the purchaser's agent under part 1311, and subpart C fixes the data the order must carry, including a nine-character tracking number the purchaser assigns in the format of the last two digits of the year, the letter X, and six characters of the purchaser's choosing. Scanning a completed paper form does not produce an electronic order, because an electronic order is valid only when it carries that DEA-issued digital signature.

Both routes run on the same sixty-day window, and it is sixty calendar days. 21 CFR 1305.13(b) lets a supplier fill a paper order in part and supply the balance by additional shipments within 60 days following the date of the form, and states flatly that no DEA Form 222 is valid more than 60 days after its execution by the purchaser. Subpart C sets the same window for an electronic order: it may be filled in part with the balance supplied within 60 days following the date of the order, and no order is valid more than 60 days after execution. The window is permission to finish an order already accepted, not permission to keep ordering, and once it closes the unshipped balance needs a new order rather than an extension. The same paragraph is also where the candidate learns that filling is discretionary: a supplier may fill the order if possible and if it desires to do so, and it records on the original its registration number where the purchaser has not entered it, the number of commercial or bulk containers furnished on each item, and the date the containers are shipped.

A defective order and a lost order are different failures with different cures, and questions are built on the seam between them. Under 21 CFR 1305.15 a paper form must not be filled if the order is not complete, legible, or properly prepared, executed or endorsed, or if it shows any alteration, erasure or change of any description; the supplier returns the original to the purchaser with a statement of the reason, the purchaser files both, and the section says in terms that a defective form may not be corrected and must be replaced by a new form before the order can be filled. Initialling an altered line, rewriting a quantity, or asking the supplier to fix the entry are three spellings of the same wrong answer, and subpart C reaches the same result electronically by providing that neither purchaser nor supplier may correct a defective order and that the purchaser must issue a new one. A lost form is not defective at all: under 21 CFR 1305.16 a purchaser who ascertains that an unfilled form has been lost executes another and attaches a statement giving the order form number and date of the lost form and stating that the goods it covered were not received through its loss.

Retention is where the two routes look most alike and behave least alike, so read which rule a question is standing on. 21 CFR 1305.17 requires DEA Forms 222 to be maintained separately from all other records of the registrant and kept available for inspection for two years, and a purchaser with several registered locations keeps the executed copy and its attachments at the registered location printed on the form. Electronic copies of Forms 222 are deemed separately maintained if they are readily retrievable separately from all other records, and they may sit on a system at a location different from the registered location so long as they are readily retrievable at the registered location. Electronic orders are preserved under subpart C's own provision rather than by cross-reference to the Form 222 rule: for each order filled the purchaser retains the original signed order and all linked records for two years, along with copies of every unaccepted or defective order and each linked statement, the supplier retains its original and linked records for two years, and records held on a central server must be readily retrievable at the registered location.

worked_examples.scenario: A supplier telephones on day 64 after your pharmacy executed a paper DEA Form 222 and offers to ship the two line items it could not supply on the first shipment. Your technician counts that only about forty-five working days have passed and asks whether the balance can still go out on the original form, since the shortfall was the supplier's back order rather than anything the pharmacy did.
steps: Identify which clock the facts are asking about. This is the 60-day window in 21 CFR 1305.13(b), which governs both the validity of the form and the period for shipping the balance of a partly filled order.

Read the unit. The paragraph says 60 days following the date of the form, and no more than 60 days after execution by the purchaser. It says days, not business days, so the technician's count of working days is not the count the regulation uses.
Fix the start point. The window runs from the purchaser's execution of the form, and nothing in the paragraph lets a supplier, a purchaser or a back order move that date.
Decide what happens to the unshipped balance. The window has closed, so the balance does not ship on the expired form; a fresh order is what puts those line items back in play.
worked_examples.resolution: The balance may not be shipped on the original form. The error the scenario invites is reading the 60 days as 60 business days, which would still be running on day 64; the second error is treating a supplier back order as something that extends a form the regulation makes invalid by its own terms.

worked_examples.scenario: A paper DEA Form 222 reaches the supplier on day 20 after execution. The form is well inside its validity period, but the purchaser wrote over one Schedule II quantity after signing. The purchaser offers to initial the change so the order can ship today rather than wait for a replacement, and points out that there is still more than a month left on the form.
steps: Split the two questions. Timeliness lives in 21 CFR 1305.13(b) and defect lives in 21 CFR 1305.15, and a form can satisfy one while failing the other.
Apply the defect test. An order showing any alteration, erasure or change of any description must not be filled, and writing over a signed quantity is exactly such a change.

Ask whether the defect can be cured. The section says a defective DEA Form 222 may not be corrected and must be replaced by a new form for the order to be filled, so an initial from the purchaser cures nothing.

Follow the routing the regulation sets. The supplier returns the original to the purchaser with a statement as to the reason, and the purchaser keeps the returned original and the statement in its files.
worked_examples.resolution: The order does not ship on this form; the purchaser executes a replacement. The error the scenario invites is letting a healthy 60-day clock stand in for validity, as though a form still inside its window could not also be one the supplier is forbidden to fill.

worked_examples.scenario: Your pharmacy mailed an executed paper DEA Form 222 to its supplier three weeks ago. The supplier says the form never arrived and that no Schedule II goods were shipped, and the pharmacy cannot produce the original. The stock is still needed, and a colleague suggests faxing the supplier the retained copy so the order can be filled from that instead.
steps: Name the failure. The form is unfilled and lost, not defective, so 21 CFR 1305.16 rather than 21 CFR 1305.15 supplies the procedure.

Execute a replacement. The purchaser executes another DEA Form 222 and attaches a statement containing the order form number and date of the lost form and stating that the goods it covered were not received through the loss of that form.

Place the copies where the regulation puts them. A copy of the second form and a copy of the statement are retained with a copy of the first form, and a copy of the statement goes to the supplier attached to a copy of the second form.

Plan for the original resurfacing. If the supplier to whom the first form was directed later receives it, the supplier marks 'Not accepted' upon the face and returns the original to the purchaser, who attaches it to the statement.

Read the reporting paragraph before adding a report. The immediate report of a lost or stolen order form, made with the serial number of each form to the Special Agent in Charge of the DEA divisional office for the registrant's area, is written for used or unused forms lost or stolen other than in the course of transmission, and this form went missing in transmission.
worked_examples.resolution: The regulation's answer to a lost unfilled form is a freshly executed form with the required statement attached, not the retained copy. The error the scenario invites is treating the retained copy as a substitute original; the subtler error is reaching for the immediate loss report without reading the carve-out the paragraph writes into it.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy scans its executed DEA Forms 222 into the same document store it uses for invoices and delivery notes, and relies on a keyword search to pull a form when an inspector asks. The same pharmacy keeps those scans on a server at the chain's head office in another state. The manager asks whether either arrangement is a problem, and whether CSOS orders can simply be filed the same way.
steps: Start with the separateness requirement. 21 CFR 1305.17 requires DEA Forms 222 to be maintained separately from all other records of the registrant and kept available for inspection for two years.

Apply the electronic deeming rule to the commingled store. Electronic copies count as separately maintained only if they are readily retrievable separately from all other records, so mixing them into a general store and sweeping it by keyword does not meet the test.

Apply the off-site rule to the head-office server. Electronic copies may be stored on a system at a location different from the registered location, provided they are readily retrievable at the registered location.

Answer the CSOS half on its own provision. Electronic orders are preserved under subpart C, which requires the purchaser to retain each original signed order and all linked records for two years and requires central-server records to be readily retrievable at the registered location.
worked_examples.resolution: The head-office server is permissible so long as retrieval at the registered location works; the commingled store is not, because readily retrievable separately is the test. The error the scenario invites is hearing readily retrievable and dropping the word separately that qualifies it, and then assuming the Form 222 preservation rule is also the rule for CSOS orders.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 21 CFR 1305.03 attach the order requirement to, and what are the two acceptable instruments?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Each distribution of a Schedule I or II controlled substance; either a DEA Form 222 or its electronic equivalent under subpart C of part 1305 and part 1311.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name three movements 21 CFR 1305.03 excepts from the order requirement.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Any three of: distributions to persons exempted from registration; conforming exports; deliveries to a registered analytical laboratory or its DEA-approved agent; delivery from a central fill pharmacy to a retail pharmacy; deliveries to an authorized registrant by an ultimate user, by a long-term care facility on behalf of a resident or former resident, or by a person authorized to dispose of a decedent's property; distributions to reverse distributors and distributors by collectors and law enforcement; and deliveries from ultimate users for a recall.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Sixty days from what event, and sixty days of which kind?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Sixty calendar days from the purchaser's execution of the form; the same window bounds the supplier's shipment of the balance of a partly filled order.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A supplier is asked to initial an altered quantity on an otherwise timely Form 222. What does 21 CFR 1305.15 require?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The form must not be filled; the supplier returns the original with a statement as to the reason, and the defective form may not be corrected but must be replaced by a new form for the order to be filled.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What two things must the statement attached to a replacement Form 222 contain after a loss?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The order form number and date of the lost form, and a statement that the goods it covered were not received through the loss of that form.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which losses of order forms trigger the immediate report, to whom, and which losses are carved out?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Theft or loss of used or unused forms by a purchaser or supplier triggers an immediate report on discovery, stating the serial number of each form, to the Special Agent in Charge of the DEA divisional office responsible for the registrant's area; losses in the course of transmission are carved out of that paragraph.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: An electronic copy of a Form 222 sits in the pharmacy's general document store. Which word in the test does that arrangement fail?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Separately. Electronic copies are deemed separately maintained only if they are readily retrievable separately from all other records.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long is an electronic order kept, by whom, and what does the rule add for a central server?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Two years by the purchaser, covering the original signed order and all linked records for each order filled plus copies of unaccepted or defective orders and their linked statements, and two years by the supplier; records on a central server must be readily retrievable at the registered location.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must a CSOS order carry that a paper form does not, and what may it contain besides Schedule II items?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A digital signature DEA issued to the purchaser or the purchaser's agent, and a nine-character purchaser-assigned tracking number formed from the last two digits of the year, the letter X, and six characters of the purchaser's choosing; the order may also include substances outside Schedules I and II and non-controlled substances.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Within what period must a supplier report a filled electronic order to DEA?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Two business days, forwarding either a copy of the electronic order or an electronic report of it in a format DEA specifies.

quick_review.text: Either a DEA Form 222 or its electronic equivalent under subpart C of part 1305 and part 1311 is required for each distribution of a Schedule I or II controlled substance, subject only to the movements 21 CFR 1305.03 excepts.

Those exceptions include delivery from a central fill pharmacy to a retail pharmacy and deliveries to an authorized registrant by an ultimate user or by a long-term care facility on behalf of a resident or former resident.

21 CFR 1305.13(b) permits partial filling with the balance supplied within 60 days following the date of the form, and makes no DEA Form 222 valid more than 60 days after its execution by the purchaser.

The same paragraph leaves filling to the supplier's discretion, and requires the supplier to record on the original its registration number where the purchaser has not entered it, the number of commercial or bulk containers furnished on each item, and the date the containers are shipped.
A DEA Form 222 must not be filled if the order is not complete, legible, or properly prepared, executed or endorsed, or if it shows any alteration, erasure or change of any description.
A defective DEA Form 222 may not be corrected; it must be replaced by a new form for the order to be filled, and the supplier returns the original to the purchaser with a statement as to the reason.
A lost unfilled DEA Form 222 is answered by executing another form with a statement giving the lost form's order form number and date and confirming that the goods it covered were not received.

Theft or loss of used or unused DEA Forms 222, other than in the course of transmission, is reported immediately upon discovery, stating the serial number of each form, to the Special Agent in Charge of the DEA divisional office responsible for the registrant's area.

DEA Forms 222 are maintained separately from all other records of the registrant and kept available for inspection for two years, and a purchaser with several registered locations keeps the executed copy and its attachments at the registered location printed on the form.

Electronic copies of Forms 222 are deemed separately maintained if readily retrievable separately from all other records, and may be stored at another location provided they are readily retrievable at the registered location.
An electronic order is valid only if signed with a digital signature DEA issued to the purchaser or the purchaser's agent under part 1311, and it must carry the data fields subpart C lists.
A supplier may not endorse an electronic order to another supplier to fill, and a defective electronic order may not be corrected by either side; the purchaser issues a new order.

On receiving a shipment against an electronic order the purchaser creates a record of the quantity of each item received and the date received, electronically linked to the original order and archived.

decision_logic.condition: Schedule I or II stock is being distributed to the pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Require a DEA Form 222 or a digitally signed electronic order unless the movement is one 21 CFR 1305.03 excepts, such as delivery from a central fill pharmacy to a retail pharmacy.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy is choosing between the paper and the electronic route.
decision_logic.action: Treat them as alternatives rather than as an original and a copy: a scan of a completed Form 222 is not an electronic order, because an electronic order must be signed with a DEA-issued digital signature and carry the fields subpart C lists.

decision_logic.condition: A supplier proposes to ship the balance of a partly filled order.
decision_logic.action: Count 60 calendar days from the purchaser's execution. Inside the window the balance may go; outside it the order is no longer valid and a new order is needed.

decision_logic.condition: The order in hand is incomplete, illegible, improperly prepared or executed, altered or erased.
decision_logic.action: Do not fill it and do not correct it. On the paper route the original goes back to the purchaser with a statement as to the reason; on either route the purchaser executes a new order.

decision_logic.condition: An unfilled order cannot be produced and the goods were never received.
decision_logic.action: Execute another order and attach the statement 21 CFR 1305.16 requires; on the electronic route give the supplier a signed statement carrying the lost order's tracking number and date and link the replacement and the statement to the record of the first order.

decision_logic.condition: Order forms are found to be missing from the pharmacy's stock of blanks.
decision_logic.action: Report the loss immediately upon discovery, stating the serial number of each form, to the Special Agent in Charge of the DEA divisional office for the area, and notify that office at once if a form is later recovered or found.

decision_logic.condition: Ordering records are being filed, scanned or migrated to a new system.
decision_logic.action: Keep Forms 222 separate from all other records and available for inspection for two years and apply the readily-retrievable-separately test to electronic copies; preserve electronic orders and their linked records for two years under subpart C rather than under the Form 222 rule.

exceptions.text: 21 CFR 1305.03 excepts seven movements from the order requirement: distributions to persons exempted from registration, conforming exports, deliveries to a registered analytical laboratory or its DEA-approved agent, delivery from a central fill pharmacy to a retail pharmacy, deliveries to an authorized registrant by an ultimate user or by a long-term care facility on behalf of a resident or former resident or by a person authorized to dispose of a decedent's property, distributions to reverse distributors and distributors by collectors and law enforcement, and deliveries from ultimate users for a recall.

21 CFR 1305.13(b) states the 60-day limit subject to an exception in paragraph (f) of the same section, under which registered procurement officers of the Defense Supply Center of the Defense Logistics Agency may take partial shipments over a period not exceeding six months and at locations other than the one printed on the form.
Subpart C carries the same Defense Supply Center exception for electronic orders, allowing shipment to other locations and partial shipments over a period not exceeding six months.

The immediate theft-or-loss report is written for used or unused forms lost or stolen other than in the course of transmission, so a form that goes missing on its way to the supplier is handled by the replacement-and-statement route instead.
An electronic order may include controlled substances outside Schedules I and II as well as non-controlled substances.

Forward a copy of each filled electronic order, or a DEA-specified electronic report of it, to DEA within two business days, and retain each original order filled with its linked records for two years.

common_traps.text: Reading the 60-day window as 60 business days, which keeps a form alive on day 64 that the regulation made invalid on day 61.
Letting a healthy 60-day clock stand in for validity, so an altered form still inside its window looks fillable.
Curing a defect by initialling the change, rewriting the quantity, or asking the supplier to correct the entry, when the regulation says a defective form may not be corrected and must be replaced.
Treating a lost order as a defective one, or a defective one as a loss, and so producing the wrong statement and the wrong file.
Attaching the immediate theft-or-loss report to a form that went missing on its way to the supplier, when the paragraph carves losses in the course of transmission out of that duty.
Hearing readily retrievable and dropping the word separately, so an electronic copy filed among invoices appears to satisfy 21 CFR 1305.17.
Treating a scan of a completed paper form as an electronic order, when an electronic order must be signed with a DEA-issued digital signature and carry the fields subpart C lists.
Applying the Form 222 preservation rule to CSOS orders, when subpart C states the electronic retention duty in its own terms.
Confusing an order with a dispensing record: the requirement attaches to a distribution between registrants, not to filling a patient's prescription.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A distribution of Schedule I or II controlled substances generally requires a DEA Form 222 or a compliant digitally signed electronic order unless a listed exception applies.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A supplier may make partial shipments on an accepted DEA Form 222 during the 60-day period after execution; the form is generally invalid after 60 days.

full_prose_under_review.title: Controlled Substance Inventory, Record Retention, and the Massachusetts Registration Term
full_prose_under_review.topic: Controlled substance inventory and record retention, with Massachusetts controlled substance registration
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Initial and biennial inventories, exact and estimated counts in opened containers, the two-year federal retention floor, and registration terms that differ by registrant type
learning_objectives: State the event that triggers the federal initial inventory, and what 21 CFR 1304.11(b) requires of a registrant that commences business with no controlled substances on hand.
Fix the biennial deadline from the previous biennial inventory date, and explain why the general-physical-inventory clause in 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) does not extend it.
Apply 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6) by asking first whether the commercial container has been opened and then which schedule the substance sits in.
State the more-than-1,000 threshold in the regulation's own units, and say which schedules it governs and which it leaves untouched.
Read 21 CFR 1304.04(a) clause by clause: which records, how long, from when, in what condition, and what its opening exception actually changes.
Separate the registrations and terms set by 247 CMR 11.05 and 247 CMR 11.06 from the federal inventory interval, so that the two two-year periods are not merged.

orientation.text: An inventory is the fixed point that the rest of a controlled-substance record system is read against. Every other record a pharmacy keeps is a record of movement, and a movement record only means something when it is anchored to a counted starting position. That is why 21 CFR 1304.11 makes a registrant take a complete inventory when it first engages in controlled-substance activity and then repeat the exercise on a fixed cycle, and why 21 CFR 1304.04(a) requires every inventory and other record required to be kept under part 1304 to be kept by the registrant and available for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration for at least 2 years from the date of that inventory or record. Read the two together: the inventory sets the anchor, and the retention rule keeps the anchor reachable long enough for someone to work forward from it.

The two federal inventory events answer different questions and are triggered by different facts. 21 CFR 1304.11(b) attaches the initial inventory to a date rather than to a delivery: every person required to keep records takes an inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand on the date he or she first engages in the manufacture, distribution, or dispensing of controlled substances, in accordance with paragraph (e) of that section as applicable. The paragraph then closes the obvious escape route by adding that a person who commences business with no controlled substances on hand shall record this fact as the initial inventory, so an empty shelf produces an inventory instead of excusing one. 21 CFR 1304.11(c) starts the recurring cycle from there: after the initial inventory is taken the registrant takes a new inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand at least every two years, and the biennial inventory may be taken on any date which is within two years of the previous biennial inventory date. The limit is measured from the previous inventory date, so a pharmacy that has let twenty-five months pass has already missed it, whatever date it now chooses.

Behind the biennial regulation sits 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1), and candidates get into trouble by reading the statute as though it enlarged the regulatory window. The statute requires a complete and accurate record of all stocks on hand every second year, except that the regulations prescribed under that section shall permit each biennial inventory following the initial one to be prepared on the registrant's regular general physical inventory date, if any, which is nearest to and does not vary by more than six months from the biennial date that would otherwise apply. That clause is an instruction to the rulemaker about coordinating the federal count with a business's own stock-taking, and the current regulation implements it by allowing any date within two years of the previous biennial inventory date. It is not a separate six-month grace period bolted onto the regulatory deadline, and treating it as one produces the wrong answer on any question that asks the candidate to count months.

How the count itself is made depends on the schedule and on whether the container has been opened, and both halves of that sentence carry weight. 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6) has a dispenser or researcher include in the inventory the same information required of manufacturers under 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iii) and (iv), which is what makes a finished-form entry name the substance, its finished form, the number of units or volume of that form in each commercial container, and the number of such commercial containers. Only then does the exact-or-estimate choice arise, and the paragraph confines it to determining the number of units of each finished form in a commercial container that has been opened. If the substance is listed in Schedules I or II the dispenser makes an exact count or measure of the contents. If it is listed in Schedule III, IV, or V the dispenser makes an estimated count or measure of the contents, unless the container holds more than 1,000 tablets or capsules, in which case an exact count is required. An unopened container is never reached by that choice at all; it is captured by the container-level entries.

21 CFR 1304.04(a) is a short paragraph in which each clause does work. Every inventory and other record required to be kept under part 1304 must be kept by the registrant, must be available for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration, and must remain so for at least 2 years from the date of such inventory or record. Three consequences follow. The clock runs from the record's own date rather than from any later event, so a fresh inventory starts a new period without ending the one still running on an older record. Two years is a floor rather than a term, which is what the words at least are doing. And availability is a live obligation rather than mere storage, so a record that exists but cannot be produced and copied on inspection has not been kept the way the paragraph asks. The exception the paragraph opens with is about location and not about duration: paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2) permit financial and shipping records such as invoices and packing slips, but expressly not executed order forms subject to 21 CFR 1305.17 and 1305.27, to be kept at a central location once the registrant has notified the Administration, and permit a registered retail pharmacy that holds additional registrations for automated dispensing systems at long term care facilities to keep those sites' records at the pharmacy. Neither paragraph shortens the two years.

The Massachusetts contribution to this section is registration rather than inventory, and it is where the arithmetic stops being uniform. 247 CMR 11.05 requires a separate controlled substance registration at each principal place of business where the licensee or registrant manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances, so a second premises is a second registration rather than an extension of the first. 247 CMR 11.06 then fixes how long a registration issued by the Board is valid, and the answer depends on who holds it. A controlled substance registration issued to a pharmacy is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year. A registration issued to an outsourcing facility is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year. A registration issued to a wholesale druggist is valid for one year beginning on December 1st of each year. The wholesale term is the one that departs, and it departs twice over, in length and in start date, which is exactly the seam a question is built on.

Two different two-year periods sit inside this section, and the surest way to lose a mark is to merge them. The federal biennial inventory interval under 21 CFR 1304.11(c) is a rolling period anchored to the registrant's own previous biennial inventory date, so it travels with the pharmacy and can land on any day of the calendar. The Massachusetts pharmacy controlled substance registration term under 247 CMR 11.06 is a fixed calendar term that begins on January 1st of an even-numbered year, so it is the same period for every pharmacy in the Commonwealth and takes no account of when that pharmacy last counted its shelves. Taking an inventory does not renew a registration, and holding a current registration says nothing about whether the inventory is due. A question that places a registration date and an inventory date in the same sentence is usually asking whether the candidate can keep the two clocks apart.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy received its registration and began dispensing on a Monday with no controlled substances on the shelves; its first Schedule II and Schedule IV shipments arrived that Friday. The pharmacist in charge signed a record on the Monday stating that no controlled substances were on hand. Twenty-three months later a new pharmacist in charge reviews the files, decides that the Monday record was not really an inventory because nothing was counted, and proposes to take what he calls the pharmacy's first inventory on the second anniversary of the Friday delivery.
steps: Read what 21 CFR 1304.11(b) attaches the initial inventory to. It is the date the person first engages in the manufacture, distribution, or dispensing of controlled substances, which here is the Monday the pharmacy began dispensing and not the Friday the stock arrived.

Give the zero-stock sentence its effect. The same paragraph says that a person who commences business with no controlled substances on hand shall record this fact as the initial inventory, so the Monday record is the initial inventory rather than a substitute for one.

Start the recurring cycle where 21 CFR 1304.11(c) starts it. The biennial duty runs after the initial inventory is taken, so the clock began on the Monday and the next inventory may be taken on any date which is within two years of that date.

Convert that into a date on the calendar. Two years from the Monday, not two years from the Friday delivery, and not two years from whatever later date someone now prefers to describe as the first inventory.
worked_examples.resolution: The Monday zero-stock record is the initial inventory and the two-year cycle runs from it, so the proposed date falls outside the window. The error the scenario invites is treating an inventory that records nothing on hand as no inventory at all, which quietly moves the start of the biennial cycle forward to the first delivery.

worked_examples.scenario: It is inventory day at a retail pharmacy. On the counter sit an unopened 500-tablet bottle of a Schedule II product, an opened 500-tablet bottle of that same Schedule II product, an opened 1,200-capsule bottle of a Schedule IV product, and a partly used stock bottle of a Schedule III product set aside as damaged and awaiting disposal. A technician proposes to estimate everything except the Schedule II items, and suggests decanting the 1,200-capsule bottle into two smaller bottles first so that neither one is over the threshold.
steps: Separate the container-level entries from the counting question. 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6) has the dispenser include the information 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iii) requires, so the unopened bottle is recorded by its finished form, the units it contains and the number of such containers.

Apply the counting rule only where the paragraph applies it. The exact-or-estimate choice is for determining the number of units of each finished form in a commercial container that has been opened, so it reaches the opened Schedule II bottle and the opened Schedule IV bottle and no others here.
Take the opened Schedule II bottle. A substance listed in Schedules I or II gets an exact count or measure of the contents, and the paragraph attaches no size threshold to that requirement.

Take the opened Schedule IV bottle. Schedules III, IV and V may be estimated unless the container holds more than 1,000 tablets or capsules, and 1,200 capsules is more than 1,000, so this one is counted exactly.

Do not lose the damaged Schedule III stock. 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iv), incorporated for dispensers by 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6), calls for the name of the substance, the total quantity and the reason it is being maintained, so it belongs on the inventory even though it will never be dispensed.
worked_examples.resolution: Exact counts for both opened bottles, container-level entries for the unopened one, and a separate entry for the damaged stock. The scenario invites two errors: reading the more-than-1,000 threshold as though it also licensed estimating an opened Schedule II container, and hunting for a repackaging step instead of counting the commercial container that was actually opened.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy's last controlled-substance inventory was taken twenty-five months ago. The pharmacist in charge points out that the store's regular general physical inventory falls next month and argues that federal law lets the controlled-substance count ride along with it. In the same conversation she proposes clearing filing space by shredding inventory records older than eighteen months, on the ground that the pharmacy has taken a newer inventory since.
steps: Fix the deadline before weighing the argument. 21 CFR 1304.11(c) requires a new inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand at least every two years and permits any date which is within two years of the previous biennial inventory date, so month twenty-five is already outside the limit.

Read the statute the argument leans on. 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) directs that the regulations permit the biennial inventory to be prepared on the registrant's regular general physical inventory date which is nearest to and does not vary by more than six months from the biennial date that would otherwise apply.

Ask what that clause actually does. It tells the rulemaker how to accommodate a business's own stock-taking, and the current regulation implements it by letting the registrant pick any date inside the two-year window. It is not six further months added on top of that window.

Turn to the shredding proposal on its own footing. 21 CFR 1304.04(a) requires every inventory and other record required under part 1304 to be kept and available for inspection and copying for at least 2 years from the date of such inventory or record, so a record eighteen months old is still inside the period.

Notice that a newer inventory does not release an older record. The period in 21 CFR 1304.04(a) runs from each record's own date, so taking a fresh inventory starts a new period without ending the one already running.
worked_examples.resolution: The inventory is overdue now and cannot wait for next month's general stock-take, and the eighteen-month-old records stay. The errors the scenario invites are reading the statutory six-month coordination clause as a grace period added to the regulatory deadline, and treating a newer inventory as something that discharges the retention period still running on an older one.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts owner holds a controlled substance registration for a retail pharmacy and is opening an outsourcing facility in a different city together with a wholesale drug warehouse at a third address. An administrator prepares a single renewal covering all three premises and diaries it against the pharmacy's federal biennial inventory date, reasoning that everything in controlled substances runs on a two-year cycle anchored to the last inventory.
steps: Start with how many registrations are in play. 247 CMR 11.05 requires a separate controlled substance registration at each principal place of business where the licensee or registrant manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances, so three premises means three registrations rather than one renewal.

Take the terms one registrant type at a time under 247 CMR 11.06. The registration issued to a pharmacy is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year, and the registration issued to an outsourcing facility is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year.

Notice where the third registration departs. Under 247 CMR 11.06 the registration issued to a wholesale druggist is valid for one year beginning on December 1st of each year, so it differs from the other two in length and in start date.

Detach the registration term from the inventory clock. 21 CFR 1304.11(c) measures its two years from the registrant's previous biennial inventory date, while 247 CMR 11.06 measures the pharmacy term from January 1st of an even-numbered year, so an inventory date cannot be used to diary a registration.
worked_examples.resolution: Three separate registrations, two of them running two years from January 1st of an even-numbered year and the wholesale one running a single year from December 1st. The errors the scenario invites are folding several principal places of business into one registration, and letting a familiar federal two-year inventory interval stand in for a Massachusetts term that is fixed by the calendar and varies by registrant type.

quick_review.text: The initial inventory is taken on the date the person first engages in the manufacture, distribution, or dispensing of controlled substances, and covers all stocks of controlled substances on hand.
A person who commences business with no controlled substances on hand records that fact as the initial inventory, so the duty is discharged by a record rather than skipped.

21 CFR 1304.11(b) takes the initial inventory in accordance with paragraph (e) of the section as applicable, so the content and counting rules that govern a routine inventory govern the first one too.
After the initial inventory is taken, the registrant takes a new inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand at least every two years.

The biennial inventory may be taken on any date which is within two years of the previous biennial inventory date, so the outer limit is measured from the last inventory rather than from any anniversary of registration.

21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) coordinates the biennial count with a registrant's regular general physical inventory date within six months of the otherwise applicable biennial date, but it does not authorise delaying the inventory past the regulatory two-year limit.

A dispenser's inventory includes the information required of manufacturers under 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iii) and (iv), which covers finished-form stock by container as well as damaged, defective or impure substances and stock held for quality control or extemporaneous compounding.
The exact-or-estimate choice applies only in determining the number of units of each finished form in a commercial container that has been opened.
For an opened container, a substance listed in Schedules I or II requires an exact count or measure of the contents, with no size threshold.
For an opened container, a substance listed in Schedule III, IV, or V may be estimated unless the container holds more than 1,000 tablets or capsules, in which case an exact count is required.

Every inventory and other record required to be kept under 21 CFR part 1304 must be kept by the registrant and available for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration for at least 2 years from the date of that inventory or record.
The two-year period in 21 CFR 1304.04(a) is a floor measured from each record's own date, so a later inventory neither shortens nor absorbs the period still running on an earlier record.
A separate controlled substance registration is required at each principal place of business where the licensee or registrant manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances.
A Massachusetts controlled substance registration issued to a pharmacy or to an outsourcing facility is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year.

A Massachusetts controlled substance registration issued to a wholesale druggist is valid for one year beginning on December 1st of each year, so it differs from the pharmacy term in both length and start date.

decision_logic.condition: A registrant is about to begin controlled-substance activity, whether or not stock has arrived.
decision_logic.action: Take the initial inventory on the date activity begins; if no controlled substances are on hand, record that fact as the initial inventory rather than waiting for the first delivery.

decision_logic.condition: The question asks whether a recurring inventory is overdue.
decision_logic.action: Find the previous biennial inventory date and measure two years from it, since 21 CFR 1304.11(c) permits any date within two years of that date and nothing later.

decision_logic.condition: Someone offers a registrant's regular general physical inventory date as a reason to take the controlled-substance count later.
decision_logic.action: Test the proposed date against the regulatory two-year limit first. The statutory coordination in 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) does not extend the deadline beyond two years from the previous biennial inventory.

decision_logic.condition: A container is in front of the person taking the inventory.
decision_logic.action: Ask first whether the commercial container has been opened. If it has not, record the container-level information; if it has, move to the schedule test in 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(6).

decision_logic.condition: The opened container holds a substance listed in Schedules I or II.
decision_logic.action: Make an exact count or measure of the contents, whatever the container size.

decision_logic.condition: The opened container holds a substance listed in Schedule III, IV, or V.
decision_logic.action: Estimate the count or measure, unless the container holds more than 1,000 tablets or capsules, in which case count it exactly.

decision_logic.condition: A controlled-substance record or inventory is being destroyed, archived or migrated.
decision_logic.action: Keep it for at least 2 years from its own date and keep it available for inspection and copying; do not let a newer record retire an older one still inside its period.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts registrant is adding a principal place of business.
decision_logic.action: Apply for a separate controlled substance registration for that place of business rather than treating the existing registration as covering it.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts registration term or expiry has to be worked out.
decision_logic.action: Identify the registrant type first. Pharmacy and outsourcing facility registrations run two years from January 1st of an even-numbered year; a wholesale druggist registration runs one year from December 1st.

ma_vs_federal.text: The inventory and retention duties in this section are entirely federal. Among these rules the Massachusetts contribution is registration: 247 CMR 11.05 fixes where a controlled substance registration is required and 247 CMR 11.06 fixes how long it lasts.

Both bodies of law use a two-year period, but they measure it differently. 21 CFR 1304.11(c) measures two years from the registrant's previous biennial inventory date, while 247 CMR 11.06 measures the pharmacy and outsourcing facility terms from January 1st of an even-numbered year.

The federal biennial interval is uniform across registrants, whereas the Massachusetts term is not: 247 CMR 11.06 gives a wholesale druggist one year from December 1st rather than two years from January 1st.

Federal law states the record-retention floor as at least 2 years from the date of the inventory or record under 21 CFR 1304.04(a); a Massachusetts registration term is not a retention period and does not measure how long any record is kept.

exceptions.text: Commencing business with no controlled substances on hand does not remove the initial-inventory duty. 21 CFR 1304.11(b) has the registrant record that fact as the initial inventory.

The statutory coordination with a regular general physical inventory in 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) is not an exception that extends the DEA deadline; the regulation gives effect to it by permitting any date within two years of the previous biennial inventory date.

Estimation is itself the exception, and it has a limit. An opened Schedule III, IV or V container may be estimated only where it does not hold more than 1,000 tablets or capsules; above that an exact count is required, and Schedules I and II are outside the estimation rule altogether.

The exception clause opening 21 CFR 1304.04(a) points to paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2), which govern where records may be held rather than how long. Financial and shipping records such as invoices and packing slips may sit at a central location once the Administration has been notified, and executed order forms subject to 21 CFR 1305.17 and 1305.27 are expressly excluded from that permission.

A registered retail pharmacy that possesses additional registrations for automated dispensing systems at long term care facilities may keep the part 1304 records for those additional registered sites at the retail pharmacy or another approved central location.

The wholesale druggist is the departure from the Massachusetts registration pattern: one year beginning December 1st, against two years beginning January 1st of an even-numbered year for a pharmacy and for an outsourcing facility.

timing_deadlines.event: Initial controlled-substance inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: On the date the person first engages in the manufacture, distribution, or dispensing of controlled substances
timing_deadlines.consequence: The inventory is due that day whether or not any controlled substances are on hand; if none are, that fact is recorded as the initial inventory.

timing_deadlines.event: Biennial controlled-substance inventory
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least every two years, on any date within two years of the previous biennial inventory date
timing_deadlines.consequence: Once two years have passed from the previous inventory date the registrant is out of compliance, and choosing a later convenient date does not cure it.

timing_deadlines.event: Coordination with a regular general physical inventory under 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The general inventory date nearest to and not varying by more than six months from the biennial date that would otherwise apply
timing_deadlines.consequence: The current regulation gives effect to this by permitting any date within the two-year window; it does not push the deadline past two years.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of an inventory or other part 1304 record
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least 2 years from the date of that inventory or record
timing_deadlines.consequence: The record must be kept by the registrant and available for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration throughout the period.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts controlled substance registration issued to a pharmacy
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year
timing_deadlines.consequence: The term is fixed by the calendar, so it runs to the end of the following odd-numbered year regardless of when the registration was issued or when an inventory was taken.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts controlled substance registration issued to an outsourcing facility
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year
timing_deadlines.consequence: The outsourcing facility runs on the same cycle as a pharmacy, which is why the wholesale term is the one that has to be memorised separately.

timing_deadlines.event: Massachusetts controlled substance registration issued to a wholesale druggist
timing_deadlines.timeframe: One year beginning on December 1st of each year
timing_deadlines.consequence: The term is half as long as the pharmacy term and starts eleven months earlier in the calendar, so a diary built on the pharmacy cycle will be wrong.

forms_records.text: The initial inventory is a record in its own right, and where no controlled substances are on hand the record of that fact is what satisfies 21 CFR 1304.11(b).

A dispenser's inventory entry for finished-form stock carries the information 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iii) requires: the name of the substance, each finished form, the number of units or volume of that form in each commercial container, and the number of such commercial containers.

Damaged, defective or impure substances awaiting disposal, stock held for quality control, and stock maintained for extemporaneous compounding are entered under 21 CFR 1304.11(e)(1)(iv) with the name, the total quantity, and the reason the substance is being maintained.

Every inventory and other record required under 21 CFR part 1304 is kept by the registrant and produced for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration for at least 2 years from its date.

A registrant that wishes to keep financial and shipping records centrally under 21 CFR 1304.04(a)(1) notifies the Administration in writing, and the notification states the nature of the records, the exact location where they will be kept, the name, address, DEA registration number and type of registration of the registrant, and whether the records will be in manual or computer readable form.

The Massachusetts registration is itself a per-premises record: 247 CMR 11.05 requires a separate controlled substance registration at each principal place of business, so an owner with several sites holds several registrations rather than one document listing them.

role_duties.duty: Take an inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand on the date activity first begins, and record a nil position where nothing is on hand.
Take a new inventory of all stocks of controlled substances on hand at least every two years, on a date within two years of the previous biennial inventory date.

Record the container-level information the regulation requires, then make an exact count or measure for opened Schedule I and II containers and an estimate for opened Schedule III to V containers except where more than 1,000 tablets or capsules are held.
Keep every inventory and other required record for at least 2 years from its date and keep it available for inspection and copying by authorized employees of the Administration.
Inspect and copy the registrant's inventories and other part 1304 records, which is the availability the retention paragraph is written to protect.

Hold a separate controlled substance registration at each principal place of business where it manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances, and track the term that attaches to its own registrant type.

common_traps.text: Waiting for the first shipment before taking the initial inventory, when 21 CFR 1304.11(b) fixes the inventory to the date activity begins and expressly covers the case of commencing business with nothing on hand.
Letting a wholesaler's invoice or a delivery record stand in for the initial inventory, when what the paragraph requires is the registrant's own inventory of stocks on hand.
Treating a zero-stock initial inventory as no inventory, which then moves the start of the biennial cycle forward to the first delivery.

Reading the six-month general-physical-inventory clause in 21 U.S.C. 827(a)(1) as a grace period added to the regulatory deadline, when the regulation implements it as any date inside the same two-year window.
Supposing that only Schedule II stock is inventoried biennially, when 21 CFR 1304.11(c) speaks of all stocks of controlled substances on hand.
Applying the more-than-1,000 threshold to an opened Schedule II container, when the threshold sits inside the Schedule III to V branch and Schedules I and II are always counted exactly.
Forgetting the word opened, and so estimating a sealed container or hunting for a schedule rule where the regulation only wants the container-level entries.
Repeating the threshold as more than 1,000 units when the regulation says more than 1,000 tablets or capsules.
Reading at least 2 years as exactly two years, so that a newer inventory looks like a licence to destroy an older record still inside its own period.
Hearing the exception at the front of 21 CFR 1304.04(a) as a shorter retention period, when paragraphs (a)(1) and (a)(2) address where records may sit and not how long they are kept.
Assuming one owner holds one Massachusetts controlled substance registration across several sites, when 247 CMR 11.05 requires a separate registration at each principal place of business.
Assuming a single biennial cycle governs every Massachusetts registrant, or that the wholesale druggist cycle also starts on January 1st.
Merging the two two-year periods, so that a federal inventory date is used to diary a Massachusetts registration or a current registration is taken as evidence that the inventory is not due.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A registrant takes an initial controlled-substance inventory on the date it first engages in controlled-substance activity; if the registrant commences business with no controlled substances on hand, it must record that zero-stock fact as the initial inventory.
exceptions: Starting business with zero controlled substances does not eliminate the initial-inventory record; the registrant records that none are on hand.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: After the initial inventory, a registrant must take a new controlled-substance inventory at least every two years. Current DEA regulation permits any date within two years of the previous biennial inventory; the related statutory general-physical-inventory language does not authorize delaying the DEA inventory beyond that regulatory two-year window.
exceptions: The statutory coordination with a regular general physical inventory does not extend the DEA regulatory deadline past two years from the previous biennial inventory.

authority.name: Exact and estimated controlled-substance inventory counts

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Schedule II inventory requires an exact count or measure; Schedule III through V opened containers may generally be estimated unless the container holds more than 1,000 units.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: DEA-required controlled-substance inventories and records must be maintained and available for inspection for at least two years unless another provision requires longer.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A SEPARATE controlled substance registration is required at EACH PRINCIPAL PLACE OF BUSINESS where the licensee or registrant manufactures, distributes or dispenses controlled substances. The term differs by registrant: a registration issued to a PHARMACY is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each EVEN-NUMBERED year; a registration issued to an OUTSOURCING FACILITY is valid for two years beginning January 1st of each even-numbered year; and a registration issued to a WHOLESALE DRUGGIST is valid for ONE year beginning DECEMBER 1st of each year.

full_prose_under_review.title: Securing Controlled Stock, Reporting Theft or Loss, and Disposing of It Lawfully
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Physical and personnel security of the controlled stock, the theft-or-loss report, and the permitted disposal routes with their destruction standard and records
learning_objectives: State what 247 CMR 9.21 requires of a Massachusetts pharmacy: where controlled substances are stored, the three permitted arrangements for Schedules II through V, and what the alarm, camera and barrier paragraphs demand.
Say who is responsible for pharmacy security and access to the prescription area, and who may and may not make entries in or adjustments to the Schedule II perpetual inventory.
Apply 105 CMR 700.005(B): when the screening happens, the single purpose it serves, where the documentation goes, and why the employment bar in 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) has no look-back period.
Separate a discrepancy found on a count from a reportable event, and name the two federal clocks that both start at discovery of a theft or significant loss.
List the factors 21 CFR 1301.74(c) tells a registrant to weigh in judging whether a loss is significant, and state what the paragraph says about substances that are later recovered.
Name the ways 21 CFR 1317.05(a) allows a practitioner to dispose of controlled substances in its own inventory, and identify the route that is written for non-practitioners only.
State the non-retrievable standard in 21 CFR 1317.90 and match each destination in 21 CFR 1317.95 to the two-employee procedure it carries.
Say when a DEA Form 41 is the required record of destruction under 21 CFR 1304.21(e), when it is not, and what separate use 21 CFR 1317.05(a)(4) makes of the same form.
State the reverse distributor's own registration duty, the delivery controls in 21 CFR 1317.15(b), and the 30-calendar-day destruction deadline in 21 CFR 1317.15(d).

orientation.text: Security in a Massachusetts pharmacy is a list of checkable conditions rather than a general aspiration, and 247 CMR 9.21 states them one at a time. All controlled substances are stored within the secured prescription area and in a safe and secure manner. Schedules II through V are stored in a securely locked and substantially constructed cabinet, or a similarly secured storage area, or dispersed throughout the stock of Schedule VI controlled substances in such a manner as to obstruct theft and diversion, so dispersal is a third permitted arrangement rather than a relaxation of the first two. The pharmacy maintains a centrally monitored security system that is able to detect a breach in security and is designed to prevent theft, and activates it when the pharmacy is closed. It maintains surveillance cameras in a manner designed to record theft and diversion of controlled substances, and retains video records for at least 14 days or, in the case of known or suspected theft or diversion, at least two years. A pharmacy located within another retail establishment is secured by a floor to ceiling barrier, securely locked and separately alarmed at all times when the pharmacy is closed. All drug order deliveries containing controlled substances are delivered directly to the pharmacy. None of this switches off for stock the pharmacy no longer wants, because 247 CMR 9.21(10) applies each requirement of the section to controlled substances that are expired, quarantined, or pending reverse distribution.

Who may be near the stock is settled in two places that answer different questions. 247 CMR 9.21(6) fixes responsibility inside the pharmacy: the pharmacist Manager of Record and the pharmacist on duty are responsible for pharmacy security and shall control access to the prescription area. The perpetual-inventory paragraph narrows that further, providing that an inventory adjustment resulting from a discrepancy is performed only by the pharmacist Manager of Record, or in the Manager of Record's absence by a pharmacist designee who then reports to the Manager of Record, that an unlicensed individual may not make any entry into or adjust the perpetual inventory, and that a certified pharmacy technician may make entries. 105 CMR 700.005(B) governs the earlier question of who is hired at all. All applicants and registrants shall screen before employment new employees who may work in or around areas where controlled substances are handled; under 105 CMR 700.005(B)(1) that screening is made solely for the purpose of determining whether the prospective employee is a responsible person who can be trusted to work in and around controlled substances, and documentation of the screening is made available to the Commissioner upon his or her request rather than filed in advance. 105 CMR 700.005(B)(2) then states a bar: no registrant shall knowingly employ any agent or employee who has had an application for registration denied for violation of any law or regulation, or has had his or her registration revoked for violation of any law or regulation, at any time. The closing words carry the weight, because they leave no look-back period against which clean years could run.

A missing quantity is not automatically a reportable event, and the sequence matters. 247 CMR 9.21(8)(c) requires a pharmacy to reconcile the perpetual inventory for each Schedule II controlled substance at least once every ten days by performing an accurate physical count of inventory on hand and comparing it with the perpetual inventory, and it then puts the next step on one person: the Manager of Record shall investigate any discrepancy and report any significant loss or suspected theft in accordance with federal and state requirements. The federal requirement appears at 21 CFR 1301.74(c). The registrant must notify the Field Division Office of the Administration in his or her area, in writing, of any theft or significant loss of any controlled substances within one business day of discovery of the theft or loss, and must also file a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 with the Administration through the DEA Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 calendar days after discovery. Those are two duties running on two clocks, not one duty with a long deadline. The paragraph adds that thefts and significant losses must be reported whether or not the controlled substances are subsequently recovered or the responsible parties are identified and action taken against them, and it allocates in-transit losses: unless the theft or loss occurs during an import or export transaction, the supplier is responsible for reporting an in-transit loss by its agent or by the common or contract carrier it selected, within one business day of discovery. Significance is judged rather than counted, against the factors the paragraph supplies: the actual quantity lost in relation to the type of business, the specific substances lost, whether the loss can be associated with access by specific individuals or attributed to unique activities, a pattern of losses over a specific time period with the results of efforts taken to resolve them, and, if known, whether the substances are likely candidates for diversion together with local trends and other indicators of diversion potential.

Disposal is not ordinary waste handling with extra paperwork. It is a separate scheme with its own part of the regulations, its own permitted destinations and its own witnessing rules, so the answer cannot be reached by asking what is convenient or what the state's waste rules would tolerate. 21 CFR 1317.05(a) opens with a closed list: a registered practitioner in lawful possession of a controlled substance in its inventory that desires to dispose of that substance shall do so in one of the following ways. Those ways are prompt destruction in accordance with subpart C of part 1317 using an on-site method of destruction; prompt delivery to a reverse distributor's registered location, by common or contract carrier pick-up or by reverse distributor pick-up at the registrant's registered location; prompt delivery, for the purpose of return or recall, to the registered person from whom the substance was obtained, to the registered manufacturer of the substance, or to another registrant the manufacturer has authorized to accept returns or recalls on its behalf; and a request for assistance from the Special Agent in Charge of the Administration in the area in which the practitioner is located. A retail pharmacy is a practitioner for these purposes, as 21 CFR 1317.05 says in terms when it describes collectors that are practitioners as retail pharmacies and hospitals or clinics. The route that lets a registrant carry the substances to the destruction site by its own means is written into 21 CFR 1317.05(b) for non-practitioners, and so is not on the practitioner's list.

Whichever route is chosen, the destruction standard and the record are fixed. 21 CFR 1317.90 requires all controlled substances to be destroyed by a registrant, or caused to be destroyed by a registrant under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), to be destroyed in compliance with applicable Federal, State, tribal and local laws and regulations and to be rendered non-retrievable. Where multiple controlled substances are comingled the method must be sufficient to render all of them non-retrievable, and where the substances collected for destruction are unknown but may reasonably include controlled substances the method must be sufficient to render non-retrievable any controlled substance likely to be present. Non-retrievable is a defined term for the purposes of the disposal part: the substance's physical or chemical condition or state is permanently altered through irreversible means, so that it is unavailable and unusable for all practical purposes and cannot be transformed back into a controlled substance or a controlled substance analogue. 21 CFR 1317.95 then attaches two employees to every destination, and 21 CFR 1304.21(e) attaches the record to only two of them: any registered person that destroys a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(d), or causes the destruction of a controlled substance under 21 CFR 1317.95(c), shall maintain a record of destruction on a DEA Form 41 that is complete and accurate and includes the name and signature of the two employees who witnessed the destruction. Massachusetts layers its own record on top: 247 CMR 9.21(9) requires a pharmacy to maintain an accurate record of all controlled substances returned to a reverse distributor or disposed of in accordance with state and federal laws and regulations, including proper DEA forms in the case of Schedule II controlled substances.
